transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, I'm here because... well, honestly, everything is just a giant mess right now and I feel like I'm completely drowning. I'm taking classes, but I also have this little accessories shop that I run—I make these custom resin pieces and beaded phone charms and stuff, which I really love doing, it's super fun to make them—but I am trying to keep up with my schoolwork at the exact same time and I just... I absolutely cannot get them organized. Like, at all. 

My room and my desk are just completely covered in these huge, random piles. I'll have my shop supplies, like my jump rings and clasps and packaging, mixed up with my shipping receipts, and then right in the middle of that is a syllabus or my assignment notes for a class. And I look at these piles, and I just stand there because I literally don't know what to do first. Like, do I sort the beads? Do I write the essay? Do I log the receipts? I even bought all these colorful plastic bins at Target last week thinking that would be the magic fix, but then I just ended up stacking the empty bins in piles too! It's just so frustrating because I can't keep track of my due dates for school or my orders for the shop, and I just stare at the mess and have no idea where to even begin.
Do you find yourself thinking about organizing or fixing the mess even when you're not actively trying to work on it?

Um, honestly? No, not really. I mean, you would think I would, right? Because it stresses me out so incredibly much when I'm sitting there looking at it. But it's actually the exact opposite. The second I walk out of my room, it's like the mess just completely evaporates from my brain. Like, out of sight, out of mind, literally. 

Yesterday, for example, I went out to grab coffee with my friend Maya—we went to this cute little place that just opened downtown and they have these amazing iced matcha lattes, which is funny because I normally don't even like matcha, it usually tastes like grass to me, but theirs is so good—and anyway, we were sitting there on the patio for like two hours, and I didn't think about my desk, or the beads, or the shipping receipts even a single time. Not once! I definitely wasn't sitting there planning out how to use those plastic Target bins or strategizing how to tackle the piles. I was just talking a million miles a minute about whatever else was going on and watching people walk their dogs. 

It’s really only when I open my bedroom door and physically step back inside and see the disaster staring me in the face that the panic just hits me all over again. But when I'm not in the room? No, I'm definitely not thinking about organizing it or fixing it. I'm usually just completely caught up in whatever else is right in front of me at that exact moment, so the mess just kind of ceases to exist until I'm trapped with it again.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Oh my gosh, yes. Constantly. It's actually a huge problem, especially with school. Like, when I have to sit through lectures—especially my history class, which is an hour and fifteen minutes long and the professor just stands at the podium and talks in this super monotone voice without even using slides—I literally cannot keep my body still. My leg will start bouncing up and down, like, vibrating against the desk, and half the time I don't even realize I'm doing it until the person sitting next to me gives me this annoyed look because I'm shaking the whole row of seats. 

And if it's not my leg, it's my hands. I'm always clicking a pen, just click-click-click, or taking the cap off and putting it back on over and over again. Or, because I have all my shop stuff with me usually, I'll have my hands in my bag just messing with stray beads or spinning the key rings around my fingers. I'll be sitting in a study group meeting at the library, and everyone else is just sitting there normally, looking at their notes, and I'm practically doing gymnastics in my chair, shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, playing with my jewelry, picking at my cuticles... it's like I have this motor inside me that just never shuts off. It's honestly exhausting, but if I try to force myself to sit completely still, I feel this horrible, tight, crawling sensation under my skin, like I'm going to explode if I don't move something. So yeah, I'm always fidgeting, even before I notice I'm doing it.
Do you ever have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to focus on something else?

Um, repeating thoughts? Like, getting stuck on something? Not really. I mean, my brain is definitely always going a million miles a minute, but it's more like a pinball machine than a broken record, if that makes sense. Like, I'm never just sitting there thinking the exact same thought over and over and over again, unable to stop it. 

It's more like... okay, so if I'm trying to focus on writing a paper for my sociology class, my brain won't get stuck on one specific thought about the paper or something bad that happened. Instead, it'll be like, "I need to write this paragraph. Oh, my water bottle is empty, I should fill it. Wait, did I respond to that girl on Instagram who wanted the cherry blossom phone charm? I need to order more of those pink beads. I wonder if the post office is still open. I should check my tracking numbers. Oh, look, a squirrel outside the window!" 

So it's just this constant stream of completely different, random things popping into my head and pulling my attention away, rather than one specific thought that just keeps looping and looping. I don't really get those repetitive, intrusive thoughts that I can't shake. It's just that my attention is constantly jumping from one shiny new thought to the next before I can even finish the first one. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I have thoughts that repeat like that. It's more of a chaotic jumble of everything all at once.
Do you often find yourself leaving tasks unfinished?

Oh, absolutely. All the time. Leaving things unfinished is basically my signature move at this point. It's like I have all the best intentions when I start something, but getting across the finish line is just... it's like hitting a brick wall. 

Like, okay, if a teacher gives me a multi-step assignment, or even if I'm on a call with one of the vendors I get my jewelry supplies from—which, by the way, I had this whole meeting with a new vendor last week because my old one stopped carrying the specific gold-plated clasps I use, and it was a whole ordeal trying to find someone who sells them in bulk without charging ridiculous shipping fees—but anyway, if someone gives me a list of things to do, I am so good at jumping right in and doing that very first step. I'll get the first part done super fast. But then... I don't know, it's like my brain just checks out, or I get distracted by the next shiny thing, and I completely drop the ball on the rest of it. 

I'll think I'm totally done, and then a day or two later I'll find out I completely skipped something super important. Like, I'll write a whole email for school but forget to attach the actual form they asked for, or with my shop, I'll pack up an order and completely forget to finish the last part of the order note, or I won't put the little freebie stickers in the package, which is something I really pride myself on doing! It's so frustrating because I'm not doing it on purpose, and it makes me look careless, but I literally just... I do step one, and then steps two and three just vanish into thin air. I'll have half-finished projects literally everywhere. Half-read books, half-painted canvases, half-organized bead boxes... it's a mess.
Do you have trouble waiting for your turn in lines or when speaking with others?

Oh, waiting is... it's the absolute worst. I am so bad at it. It's almost physically painful, if that makes sense? Like, standing in lines, oh my gosh. The financial aid office at school is a nightmare for this. Every semester, there's some issue with my paperwork—probably because I forgot step two of a three-step process, like we just talked about—and I have to go stand in that line. And it's always snaking out the door, and the people at the desk move so slowly. I'll be standing there, and I literally cannot just stand. I'm shifting my weight from one foot to the other, I'm checking my phone, putting it away, checking it again, sighing, taking my backpack off, putting it back on. I get so overwhelmingly impatient that I feel like I'm going to crawl out of my own skin. 

And it's not just physical lines, it's talking, too. Like in my art classes, when we have group critiques? Everyone is supposed to take a turn talking about a piece, and you have to wait for the person before you to finish their thought. But if I have an idea, or if I notice something about the shading or the composition, it's right there at the tip of my tongue, and holding it in feels impossible. I'll literally be bouncing on my heels, practically vibrating, just waiting for them to take a breath. And honestly, half the time I don't even wait. I just blurt it out. I'll just cut right in before I even realize I'm doing it. 

Or like, if I need to ask a professor a question after class, and there are two other students in front of me? I'm just hovering there, practically pacing in a tiny circle, trying to force myself not to just interrupt their conversation because my question will only take two seconds! It's just... waiting feels like wasted time, and my brain doesn't know how to handle it, so I end up squirming around and accidentally interrupting people because I just can't hold it in anymore.
Do you often find yourself losing your temper or getting really angry?

Um, losing my temper? No, not really. I mean... I get frustrated, sure, like anybody would. Like, okay, the other day I was trying to string these tiny, tiny glass seed beads for a custom necklace—they're literally like two millimeters wide, just impossibly small—and I accidentally knocked the whole plastic organizer tray off my desk. And it went everywhere. All over my floor. Which, by the way, is a white shag carpet, which was honestly a terrible design choice for my room considering what I do, I really don't know what I was thinking when I bought it at Target two years ago. 

But anyway, I was definitely annoyed, and I think I groaned and just laid on the floor for a second looking at this massive mess, but I wasn't, like, *angry* angry. I don't really have a temper. I don't yell at people or fly into a rage or anything like that. I'm actually a pretty upbeat person most of the time! And honestly, I think because my brain is always jumping to the next thing, even if I do get a tiny bit irritated about something, I literally just forget about it five minutes later. I couldn't hold a grudge if I tried because I just don't have the attention span for it. I'll be mad for two seconds and then I'll see a funny TikTok and completely forget why I was upset.

Sometimes my mom or my friends will think I'm mad because I'll be talking really loud and fast and waving my hands around, but I always have to stop and be like, "No, wait, I'm not yelling at you, I'm just really passionate and excited about this!" People misinterpret my energy for anger sometimes, which is kind of a bummer, but I'm really not mad. So, yeah, no real temper issues here. Just normal annoyance that passes super quick.
Do you have trouble focusing on tasks that require you to think carefully and pay attention for a long time?

Oh, absolutely. Like, one hundred percent. If something requires me to just sit there and focus for a long stretch, especially if it's heavy thinking? It's basically a lost cause. 

Like, I'm taking these business classes right now—mostly online modules, because I figured if I'm going to run my jewelry shop properly, I should probably learn how to actually manage the backend stuff, right? My mom told me I really needed a solid foundation for the business side of things so I don't just wing it forever. So they have these long lecture videos you have to watch for the assignments. And I'll sit down, I'll have my notebook out, my pens lined up, totally ready to go. I always start out listening so well! For the first, I don't know, three or four minutes, I am totally dialed in. 

But then the instructor will start getting into the weeds about, like, accounting software or marketing analytics, and my brain just... takes a massive detour. I'll start thinking about my shop instead. Like, I'll be picturing this new line of celestial-themed charms I want to launch, trying to decide if the little resin moons should have gold flakes or holographic glitter in them, or I'll start mentally planning out my next batch of orders and what color tissue paper I should use for the packaging. And I'll be so deep in thought about the charms that suddenly I'll blink, and the video is ten minutes further along, and I realize I completely zoned out and missed half of what was said. 

It's so incredibly frustrating. Because then I have to scrub back and rewind it, and try to find the exact spot where I stopped paying attention, which is hard because I don't even know when my brain checked out in the first place! And it happens in regular in-person classes, too. If a teacher is just talking and talking without a break, I just can't hold on to the words. I'll be physically looking right at them, nodding, looking like I'm paying full attention, but inside my head I'm just mapping out how many bubble mailers I need to buy for the week. It's like my brain just cannot sustain the effort of listening to dense information for more than a few minutes before it demands to think about something more fun or creative. I literally have to watch a twenty-minute video in like, five different chunks just to actually hear all of it.
Do you have trouble calming down when you're upset?

Um, no, not really. Actually, it's kind of the opposite? Like I was saying before about the temper thing, I just don't hold onto negative emotions for very long at all. 

Like, okay, just last week, I was working on this huge batch of custom resin keychains for the shop. I do these really elaborate floral ones where I have to dry the flowers myself. I press them in these heavy books for weeks—usually old textbooks I never returned, which, honestly, the late fees on those were ridiculous, but they make great flower presses. But anyway, I spent hours arranging these tiny dried daisies and gold flakes into the molds. And then I poured the resin, and I guess I didn't seal the edges of this one new mold I bought online, and it just... leaked everywhere. Just a sticky, toxic mess all over my favorite pink silicone desk mat. 

And I was so upset. Like, I literally put my head down on my desk and just started crying because I was so overwhelmed and it felt like hours of work were just completely ruined. I was fully having a meltdown about it. 

But then, I don't know, maybe two minutes into crying, my cat, Barnaby—he's this massive orange tabby who has absolutely zero spatial awareness—he jumped up onto the desk and almost stepped right in the wet resin! And I had to scoop him up so fast, and he made this ridiculous little squeaking noise, and I just... started laughing. And just like that, I wasn't upset anymore. The crisis was over. I just grabbed the paper towels and some rubbing alcohol and started cleaning it up, totally fine. 

My mom always tells people that my bad moods are like a summer storm, where it pours rain for five minutes and then the sun is just completely back out like nothing happened. I just get distracted by the next thing I have to do, or something funny happens, and my brain completely shifts gears. So calming down is actually pretty easy for me, mostly because I just literally forget that I was even crying in the first place!
Do you often struggle to motivate yourself to start tasks or activities?

Um, no? Not really. Honestly, it's usually the exact opposite for me. If I get an idea to do something, I am starting it right that exact second. Motivation is never really the issue. It's almost like... over-motivation? If that makes sense? 

Like, just the other night, it was maybe 11:30 PM, and I was supposed to be winding down, but I was scrolling on Pinterest and I saw these really gorgeous, intricate wire-wrapped crystal pendants. And instead of just pinning the picture to my inspiration board and going to sleep like a normal person, I literally jumped right out of bed, turned all the lights back on, and dragged out my entire bin of copper wire. Which, by the way, I have a ridiculous amount of, because I bought it in bulk like a year ago when I thought I was going to get really into making outdoor wind chimes—which I never actually did, but that's a whole different story. 

But anyway, I just grabbed my pliers and my amethyst stones and I just dove right in. I didn't even have a sketch or a plan or anything, I just started twisting wire and seeing what happened. I was sitting there on my bedroom floor in my pajamas until probably 3 AM, just totally energized and ready to go. When I get a burst of inspiration, I just *have* to start doing it immediately. The energy just takes over. 

So, yeah, starting things is super easy for me! I don't really sit around trying to hype myself up to do stuff or feel stuck. If anything, my mom is always telling me I need to slow down and actually think for two seconds before I launch into a brand new project, because my room always ends up looking like a craft store exploded since I just jump straight into things. But if I want to do something, I'm doing it right then and there. I don't really struggle with getting started at all.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Oh my gosh, yes. It is honestly one of my worst habits and I hate that I do it. It's like my brain is moving faster than the other person's mouth, if that makes sense? I don't ever mean to be rude, I really don't, but it happens all the time, especially in group critiques or class discussions. 

Like, for my jewelry stuff, I sometimes do these local artisan workshops, and we have these group critique circles where we sit around and look at everyone's progress. And someone will be talking, giving feedback or asking a question, and I just... I jump in with my answer before the other person is even done talking! I'll just completely cut them off. Like last week, this girl Sarah was talking about her wire wrapping, and she was explaining how she was having trouble getting the thicker gauge copper to do something, and before she could even finish her thought about bending it, I just blurted out loud that she needed to heat it with a torch first to soften it. 

And then I just feel so incredibly embarrassed. Because I realize I just guessed what they were going to say, and I totally hijacked their moment. And sometimes I'm right about what they were going to ask, but sometimes I'm completely wrong and they were going in a totally different direction entirely, which makes it even worse! And everyone just kind of stops and looks at me, and I have to do this whole awkward backpedaling thing where I apologize profusely and tell them to please keep going and pretend I didn't just interrupt them. 

It just happens so fast. I get so excited to share the answer, or I think I know exactly what point they are trying to make, and I literally cannot hold the words inside my mouth. It feels like this physical pressure building up until I just spit it out. My mom gets so annoyed with me at dinner too because I constantly finish her sentences, but the class critiques are where it really gets to me because I want to seem professional and respectful, you know? But I just end up blurting things out anyway like I can't wait my turn.
Do you often blurt out answers before the teacher or others have finished asking a question in class?

Yeah, that's exactly what I was just saying! It's literally that exact same thing. Whether it's those group critiques for my jewelry making or just general class discussions—like back when I was in regular high school classes, oh my gosh, it was a nightmare for my teachers. I just... I completely jump in with my answer before the other person is even done talking. 

Because, like I said, I just sit there and I guess what they're going to say. My brain just kind of fast-forwards to the end of their question, and I'm so sure I know what they're asking that the answer just flies out of my mouth. Like, I can't even stop it. And then, of course, the teacher or whoever is talking just stops dead in their tracks, and the whole room gets quiet, and I instantly feel so, so embarrassed. Because I realize in that moment that I just completely guessed what they were asking, and half the time they were actually going to ask something completely different! 

Like, I remember in my senior year history class, Mr. Davis was asking this long, drawn-out question about the Industrial Revolution, and he paused to take a breath, and I just shouted out "The cotton gin!" from the back row. And he just looked at me and was like, "No, I was asking about child labor laws." And I just wanted to melt into a puddle on the floor right then and there. It's just... I get so eager, I guess? Or I just don't have a filter between my brain and my mouth. But yeah, just like with the interrupting thing I was just talking about, I just blurt it out and then have to sit there feeling totally mortified because I couldn't just wait two more seconds for them to actually finish their sentence.
Do you find it hard to stick with an activity until it's finished?

Oh, absolutely. It's... it's honestly so frustrating because I really do want to finish things, but my brain just will not cooperate. Especially if the activity is something where I have to just sit and pay attention to someone talking. 

Like... well, right now I'm trying to figure out how to actually sell all this jewelry I make, right? So I have these online videos I have to watch for these business assignments. And I always start out with the best intentions. I'll sit down at my desk, I'll have my notebook open, I'll have a fresh pen, and I tell myself I'm going to get through the whole thing and take really good notes. And I do start out listening, I really do. But then, literally just a few minutes in, my mind is just... gone. 

I'll start thinking about these new charm designs I want to try making—like these little resin mushrooms I saw a tutorial for, or maybe doing a whole celestial collection with tiny silver stars and crescent moons—or I'll start brainstorming order ideas and how I could package them with custom tissue paper and those little personalized thank-you stickers. And I get so deep into planning all of that out in my head, visualizing exactly how the copper wire is going to wrap around the quartz, that I completely tune out the screen. And then suddenly I'll snap back to reality and realize the video has been playing this whole time and I missed half of what was said! 

It's exactly how I used to be back in regular classes, too. I'd start out listening to the teacher, and then five minutes later I'm mentally designing a necklace or thinking about my supplies, and I have absolutely no idea what lesson we're on or what they just spent the last twenty minutes talking about. It takes me forever to finish one simple business video because I have to keep pausing and rewinding it, and even when I do rewind it, I usually end up drifting off again at the exact same part because my brain just wants to go back to the charm designs! So yeah, sticking with something until the end is really, really hard for me unless my hands are physically moving.
Do you find it hard to control your emotions when something is frustrating you?

No, not really. I mean, I definitely get frustrated, obviously, like everyone does, but I don't think I have a hard time controlling my emotions about it. Like, if I'm working on a piece of jewelry and the wire just won't bend the way I want it to, or if I accidentally snap a delicate chain that I just spent an hour assembling, I get super annoyed, sure. I might sigh really loudly or just drop my pliers on the desk and walk away for a minute to get a snack or something. 

But I don't, like, throw things across the room or scream or completely lose my temper, you know? I just kind of huff about it and then move on to a different project or take a break. Like yesterday, I was trying to do this really intricate weave with some sterling silver wire, which is so expensive by the way, and I messed up the pattern right in the middle. I was so mad because I basically had to scrap the whole piece and start over, and I definitely complained about it to my mom for like ten minutes straight, just venting about how annoying it was and how much money I just wasted. But I wasn't like, crying or having a meltdown or anything. I just talked her ear off about it until I felt better, and then I went back and tried again. So yeah, I feel like I handle frustration pretty normally, I just might be a little dramatic when I vent about it sometimes.
Do you find it challenging to maintain your focus over a long period of time when working on a task that requires continuous mental effort?

Well, yeah, that's kind of exactly what I was just getting at with those videos! It's like... anything that requires me to just sit there and focus my brain on one continuous stream of information is my absolute worst enemy. 

Whether it was back in regular classes in high school, or now when I'm watching a video for my business assignments, it always plays out the exact same way. I really do try—I can start out listening and I'm totally focused for the first couple of minutes, telling myself how important it is to learn about, like, marketing algorithms or whatever. But then, almost without me even realizing it's happening, my mind is just... gone. It's completely wandered off onto my charm designs, or I'm brainstorming order ideas, like figuring out if I should switch to eco-friendly mailers or how to format my shipping labels. 

And I can go on like that for ten, fifteen minutes, just completely lost in my own head, visualizing all these little details while the person on the screen or at the front of the room is still talking. And then suddenly I'll sort of blink and snap back to reality, and I realize I missed half of what was said! It's so incredibly draining because it means anything that takes continuous mental effort ends up taking me three times as long. I have to just keep rewinding the video, and rewinding it again, and hoping this time the information actually sticks, but my brain always just wants to default back to the jewelry. It's like trying to hold water in my hands. No matter how hard I try to just sustain that focus, it always slips right through.
Do you often have trouble keeping track of assignments, deadlines, or appointments?

Oh my gosh, yes. Honestly, that is the main reason I actually came in to see you in the first place. I just feel like I absolutely cannot get my schoolwork—like those business assignments I was telling you about—and my little accessories shop organized at the same time. It's like my brain just completely short-circuits when I try to juggle both of them. 

If you looked at my desk right now, or honestly even my bedroom floor, it's just... it's a total disaster. Everything just ends up in these massive, chaotic piles. I'll have my jewelry supplies, like spools of expensive silver wire and bags of tiny jump rings and half-finished resin charms, just completely mixed in with all my important papers. I've got my assignment notes from those videos buried under there, and due dates written on random sticky notes that always seem to lose their stickiness and fall behind the desk, so I completely forget when things are actually due! 

And don't even get me started on the receipts. I have all these crumpled-up receipts from the craft store because I'm supposed to be tracking my expenses for the business, but they just get shoved into the exact same pile as my school notebooks and my shipping labels. I'll sit down and look at this absolute mountain of stuff, and I just freeze. I have absolutely no idea what to do first. Do I sort the receipts? Do I try to find the due date for my marketing assignment? Do I organize the beads? I just get so overwhelmed by the piles that I end up doing none of it, or I just start making a totally new necklace because it's easier than dealing with the mess. So keeping track of deadlines and everything right now is just... yeah, it's really, really bad.
Do you find that your emotions or motivations significantly influence your ability to complete tasks or follow through on plans?

Um, I don't really think so? Like, I'm not entirely sure what you mean by emotions influencing it, because I don't really feel like my mood dictates whether I get things done or not. I hear people talk about needing to be in the right headspace or needing to feel inspired to work, especially with creative stuff like my jewelry, but for me, it's really not about that at all. 

Honestly, my motivation is usually really high! I want my little accessories shop to be super successful, which is exactly why I'm forcing myself to take those business and marketing classes in the first place, even though they're a total nightmare for my brain to sit through. I have all these big plans, like I want to expand into doing custom bridal pieces, maybe working with gold-filled chains and Swarovski crystals, which is a whole different market, you know? It takes a lot of planning and sourcing. So the drive is one hundred percent there. I'm super motivated. 

But even when I'm incredibly excited about a project—like last week, I got my very first commission for a set of matching bridesmaid bracelets, and I was absolutely thrilled, like over the moon about it—I still couldn't just sit down and finish them in one go. I was so happy and motivated, but I still ended up getting up to find a different gauge of wire, and then I saw my cat had knocked over a plant in the hallway, so I cleaned that up, and then I decided the plant actually needed to be repotted since the dirt was everywhere anyway... and before I knew it, three hours had passed and the bracelets were just sitting there half-done on my desk. 

So, yeah, it's not that I'm sad or lacking motivation or that I'm waiting for the right mood to strike. Even when I'm in the best mood ever and totally pumped to work on my business, I still just... drift off and start doing a million other things. So I wouldn't say my emotions or my motivation are the problem at all. It's just the actual sitting still and following through part that gets me, completely regardless of how I'm feeling. Does that make sense? Because I really do want to do the work, I just... don't.
Do you find it hard to focus on tasks for more than a few minutes without getting distracted?

Well, wait, didn't we just talk about this? I mean, I feel like I just explained this whole thing with the videos, right? Like, how I can only focus for a couple of minutes before my brain just totally wanders off to my jewelry designs or whatever else I'm thinking about. 

I guess... I mean, maybe you're asking about other tasks? Because it's not just the videos, it's pretty much everything. If I'm trying to read a textbook for my business class, or even if I'm just trying to read a long email from a supplier about, I don't know, a backorder on the sterling silver clasps I use—which is super frustrating, by the way, because I have orders waiting on those clasps—I just can't get through it. I'll read the first sentence, maybe the second, and then I'm just staring at the screen while my brain goes, "Oh, I wonder if I have enough padded envelopes for the orders going out tomorrow," or "I should probably check if my cat needs food." 

And then I have to go back and read the same paragraph over and over again, just like with the videos. So, yeah, I guess the answer is yes, but I really feel like I already covered this when I was talking about how hard it is to sustain my focus and how I'm always having to rewind things. I don't know, maybe I'm misunderstanding the question? It just feels like we're kind of going in circles here.
Do you often feel restless or have difficulty engaging in activities quietly, especially in situations where you need to be still?

Oh, restless? Yeah, absolutely. It's like... it's like this constant, humming feeling inside my chest and my arms, almost like my body is buzzing? Even when I'm not actually going anywhere or doing anything active, I just feel this intense, overwhelming urge that I need to be moving. 

It's the absolute worst when I'm supposed to just sit still and listen, like if I have to sit through a lecture for those business classes—which I'm doing online now, thank goodness, but even sitting at my desk is a nightmare. I'll be sitting there, trying so hard to just be quiet and absorb the information about, you know, profit margins or market research, and my leg will just start bouncing. It bounces so fast, like a jackhammer, and I don't even realize I'm doing it until the whole desk is shaking and my monitor is wobbling. 

And if I try to force myself to stop shaking my leg, then my hands start going. I'll be twisting my rings around my fingers, or grabbing a piece of scrap wire from my jewelry supplies and just bending it back and forth, back and forth, until it snaps. I just cannot just exist quietly in a chair. It feels physically uncomfortable, like an itch I can't scratch, if I'm not shifting my weight, or tapping my foot, or playing with something in my hands. Even when I'm watching a movie with my friends, I'm the one who's constantly getting up to get water, or shifting around on the couch, or crocheting while I watch, because just sitting still and quietly engaging with the movie feels impossible. The buzzing just gets too loud if I don't let it out somehow.

Do you think your difficulties with organization, time management, and sustaining focus on tasks are causing significant problems in your daily life, such as impacting your relationships, work, or overall well-being?

Oh, gosh, yeah. It's causing huge problems. Like, massive problems, actually. It's not just a little quirky thing where I'm a bit scattered, you know? It's really messing things up for me right now. 

Like, with my classes, because I can't just sit down and focus or keep track of all the deadlines and paperwork... I actually missed some required steps for my program. I'd start out listening to the teacher, and then five minutes later I'm mentally designing a necklace or thinking about my supplies, and I have absolutely no idea what lesson we're on or what they just spent the last twenty minutes talking about. It takes me forever to finish one simple business video because I have to keep pausing and rewinding it, and even when I do rewind it, I usually end up drifting off again at the exact same part because my brain just wants to go back to the charm designs! So yeah, sticking with something until the end is really, really hard for me unless my hands are physically moving.

But I wasn't like, crying or having a meltdown or anything. I just talked her ear off about it until I felt better, and then I went back and tried again. So yeah, I feel like I handle frustration pretty normally, I just might be a little dramatic when I vent about it sometimes.

Um, I don't really think so? Like, I'm not entirely sure what you mean by emotions influencing it, because I don't really feel like my mood dictates whether I get things done or not. Honestly, my motivation is usually really high! I want my little accessories shop to be super successful, which is exactly why I'm forcing myself to take those business and marketing classes in the first place, even though they're a total nightmare for my brain to sit through. I have all these big plans, like I want to expand into doing custom bridal pieces, maybe working with gold-filled chains and Swarovski crystals, which is a whole different market, you know? It takes a lot of planning and sourcing. So the drive is one hundred percent there. I'm super motivated.

patient.answer:
Oh, restless? Yeah, absolutely. It's like... it's like this constant, humming feeling inside my chest and my arms, almost like my body is buzzing? Even when I'm not actually going anywhere or doing anything active, I just feel this intense, overwhelming urge that I need to be moving.

Even when I'm watching a movie with my friends, I'm the one who's constantly getting up to get water, or shifting around on the couch, or crocheting while I watch, because just sitting still and quietly engaging with the movie feels impossible.
